title: Glory 2nd Edition - Simplicity is thy Name!
body:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zSvZdF7CBjU

Daniel (@dungeondive) takes a look at *Glory* Second Edition from Hog Publishing — possibly the most simplistic adventure game he has played, and he means it admiringly. Seven pages of rules, box to first turn in ten minutes, and yet everything the Dungeon Dive looks for survives the reduction: an overland map, a hero who grows, loot, quests, bosses, random encounters.

Two to four players roll a d8, move exactly that many spaces, and race to twenty glory. Land on a shield and you may fight — combat is a single opposed roll plus power — but you are almost never obliged to engage, which turns every encounter into a press-your-luck decision. Towns heal you and hide face-down quests; lairs hide face-down bosses; the castle sells goods. The nuance lives in three decks: abilities earned every five glory that break rules outright (teleport to a town, learn a skill on an empty space), goods that do much the same, and fate cards that fire immediately. Every card is dry-erasable, so quest progress is tracked in marker.

His reservations are longevity and art direction — each piece is lovely, but box front, card faces, board and manual look like five different games. He suspects it shines competitively, and wants many more than its six solo scenarios.

----

*Glory* never forces you into a fight — one round in, you can always walk away clean. Does opt-in combat make encounters more interesting by handing you the decision, or does the tension leak out once refusal costs nothing?
